coherence.reasons: Both run the same clean chain: bridge, why the hours cut fails, promotions, e-commerce, sized plan, sequencing. Y's executive summary maps neatly onto its sections and its lever sizes tie to the body. Y's governing thought, though, promises about 3.2% by FY2028 while its own plan page says the 2027 wage rise (before FY2028) would leave margin near 2.7%, below target, and nothing closes that gap. X's governing thought ("the 3% target is reachable") is carried through: a lever bridge to $45.6M, FY2026 phasing against the covenant, and contingency levers that offset the wage rise. X has minor blemishes (one slide title is just a number; the promotion cut is rated Medium in the lever table but counted as high-confidence in the risk table), but its hierarchy holds together better end to end.

judgment.reasons: Both recommend an R1-type plan with targeted rather than across-the-board labor changes, repriced delivery that respects the owners, and pruning of losing promotions. X weighs the trade-offs more carefully. It takes promotions only to 26% and keeps events in ValuMart areas, with a monthly comp trigger to restore them. It holds the three long-lease stores out of the base plan after showing a roughly 3.4-year payback on the $7.5M exit cost. It phases FY2026 to about $27M against the $20M covenant. It sizes the downside if only high-confidence levers deliver (about 2.0%) and adds $7.6M of contingency levers to absorb the wage rise. Y goes all the way back to 24% promotional share on the assumption that sales moved off promotion stay at regular price, which is aggressive given ValuMart. It puts all nine stores in the base without testing the payback on the three. Its covenant case clears $20M by about $0.1M (15.3 plus a quarter of 19.2). It admits the wage rise leaves the plan at 2.7% without a remedy. Y's one-time cost is left as "cost every move" rather than estimated.

evidence.reasons: Both reproduce the critical numbers correctly: margins, the percentage-point bridge with labor at 13%, the gross-margin split (−0.70 / −0.50 / +0.18), the e-commerce loss of $10.4M reconciled to the $18.1M fulfillment line, the fee test roll-out of about $3.0M gross, and $6.6M for nine store exits. Both rebut the 6.1% claim on the same two grounds. X is somewhat stronger on the category team's claim, calling it correlation as well as a sales-not-profit measure; Y says only the latter. X caveats its shrink-leak estimate as an upper bound because theft is 35% of shrink, nets the 3% rate rise out of the fee gain, and flags possible underlying drift. X's weak spots are the vendor-funding lever, which rests on an interpretive reading of the 14-point gap, and a $10M implementation allowance that is its own estimate; both are disclosed. Y's weak spots are the inference that 17% of promotional sales is less than 38% of events (mixing sales share with event count), the unsupported assumption that de-promoted sales are fully retained, and a covenant claim with almost no headroom.

revision.reasons: Both revise the wage hypothesis decisively and on the right grounds: wages up 9.4% but hours per $1,000 down 6%, so labor is only 0.3 points, or 13%, of the fall. Both show the 8% cut tops out at about 2.0% even if the full saving sticks, and that shrink would hand part of it back. Both keep a targeted labor element in the best-staffed stores and reject the e-commerce freeze in favour of repricing. Y is slightly more gracious in acknowledging that management's wage observation is true. X goes a little further in showing the draft plan's consequences: a 1.3–2.0% margin range and FY2026 operating income possibly on the covenant line. The difference is small.

overall.reasons: Both documents are strong, numerically sound and reach a defensible conclusion backed by a quantified bridge and a sized plan of about $30M. X would serve the CEO better at the board. Its plan is more conservative on the riskiest lever (promotions against ValuMart). It separates base from contingency, including the three stores that need a vote. It gives a phased FY2026 figure with real covenant headroom, estimates one-time cost against the $25M cap, and shows how the plan still clears 3.0% after the 2027 wage rise. Y is crisp and well argued, but its own numbers leave the plan near 2.7% after the wage rise, its covenant headroom is razor-thin, and its costing is deferred.
